events.title: Internet Explorer 3.0 released
events.summary: Microsoft shipped Internet Explorer 3.0 on August 13, 1996 with CSS, Java applets, ActiveX controls, and its own JavaScript implementation (JScript).
events.about: IE 3 was Microsoft's first browser that could credibly compete with Netscape on features — and it was free for all Windows users. CSS support let sites separate layout from content; ActiveX tied the web tightly to Windows, foreshadowing years of compatibility headaches.

narrative.whyChosen: IE 3 closed the feature gap and escalated the browser wars into a standards fight.
narrative.whyImportant: It brought CSS and scripting to Microsoft's massive Windows install base.
narrative.problemSolved: Netscape dominated the web; Microsoft needed a free, capable browser to keep Windows central to the internet.

events.title: Nokia 9000 Communicator released
events.summary: Nokia launched the 9000 Communicator in August 1996 — a clamshell phone that opened to reveal a QWERTY keyboard and full GeOS PDA.
events.about: The Communicator combined GSM voice with fax, email, and web browsing in one device — a blueprint for later smartphones. Executives carried them across Europe before BlackBerry conquered North American enterprise email. Mobile developers built GeOS apps and WAP services for Nokia's high-end line.

narrative.whyChosen: The 9000 Communicator was the first widely sold smartphone-form-factor device with a full keyboard and PDA software.
narrative.whyImportant: It established the 'communicator' category that Nokia dominated for a decade.
narrative.problemSolved: Mobile professionals needed phone, email, and organizer features without carrying two devices.

events.title: Amaya — W3C browser and editor
events.summary: The W3C released the first public Amaya binary on August 23, 1996 — a testbed browser and editor for emerging web standards like HTML, CSS, and MathML.
events.about: Amaya was never meant for mainstream users — it was a reference implementation where standards authors could try new specs in real software. Researchers and spec writers used it to validate CSS layout, structured editing, and semantic markup ideas before they reached commercial browsers.

narrative.whyChosen: Amaya shows how standards bodies prototyped the web platform alongside vendors.
narrative.whyImportant: It helped prove CSS and structured editing could work in a real browser, not just on paper.
narrative.problemSolved: The W3C needed a living laboratory to test specifications without waiting for Netscape or Microsoft.
